title: Fielded Max-Sim Keying for Assistant-Side Memory Recall in Long-Term Conversational Assistants

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to close the retrieval gap for single-session-assistant (SSA) queries, where users ask about information the assistant previously provided, without harming other query types. Paper [3] discusses the limitations of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems in handling extended dialogue histories and selective recall, which aligns with the general problem of improving retrieval for conversational memory. Paper [2] also identifies unique challenges in retrieving information from long-form conversational data, which includes addressing retrieval gaps in conversational contexts. Both papers share the same problem-class level objective of improving retrieval for conversational memory systems, including SSA-like scenarios.

### Mechanism
The contribution introduces "fielded max-sim keying," which treats each conversation round as a two-field document with separate embeddings for user and assistant content, scoring relevance as the maximum similarity across fields. Paper [6] discusses field-based relevance modeling for semi-structured documents, where fields are used as sources of information for relevance modeling and ranking. Paper [8] extends BM25F to proximity-based scoring of documents with multiple fields, which is conceptually similar to scoring relevance across fields. Paper [18] introduces Multi-Field Adaptive Retrieval (MFAR), a framework for retrieval using structured documents with multiple fields, which is substantively equivalent to the mechanism described in the contribution. These prior works cover the mechanism at the primitive level.

### Evaluation
The contribution evaluates its method on LongMemEval, a benchmark for long-term conversational assistant memory retrieval, and reports metrics like Recall@10 and SSA-specific metrics. Paper [1] introduces LongMemEval as a benchmark for evaluating long-term memory abilities in chat assistants, including information extraction and multi-session reasoning. Since the contribution uses the same benchmark family (LongMemEval) and similar metrics (Recall@10), the evaluation design is covered by [1].

### Domain
The contribution operates in the domain of long-term conversational assistant memory retrieval. Papers [2], [3], [5], and [27] all address long-term conversational memory retrieval in LLM-based systems, which is the same general application area. While the contribution targets SSA queries specifically, this is a narrower instance within the broader domain of conversational assistant memory retrieval, making the domain covered.
